title: The objection that wasn't about price
text:
Four meetings in, the client said it: "It's too expensive."

The old version of Kalin would have started defending. Quality, experience, results, all true and all useless. Instead he asked one question. "Too expensive compared to what?"

The answer surprised him. They weren't comparing him to a cheaper competitor. They were comparing the programme to doing nothing, because two years earlier they had paid for training that nobody attended after week three.

The objection was never price. It was risk.

So he changed the proposal, not the number. The first month became a pilot with one department. Payment for the rest depended on attendance staying above 70%. If it dropped, they could stop with no penalty.

They signed in nine days.

Attendance in the pilot was 88%, mostly because the sessions were booked into the calendar by the client's own team leader, not by Kalin.

He now asks the same question in every negotiation, and roughly half the time the word "expensive" turns out to mean something else entirely.

questions.q: What did Kalin do instead of defending his price?
options: He asked what they were comparing it to
Risk, based on a previous failed training

questions.q: How did he change the proposal?
options: A pilot with payment tied to attendance

questions.q: Why was attendance in the pilot high?
options: The client's own team leader scheduled the sessions

title: Forty prospects, nine calls
text:
The new salesperson had a list of forty prospects and a target of ten meetings a month. She spent the first week calling all forty. She got two meetings and a lot of polite refusals.

Her manager looked at the list with her on Friday. Of the forty, eleven had fewer than ten employees, so they had no training budget at all. Nine had bought from a competitor within the last three months. Six had no contact name, only a general email address.

That left fourteen worth calling, and only nine where she knew who the decision maker was.

The second week she called those nine, twice each, at different times of day. She reached seven people and booked five meetings.

Same person, same script, same voice. The difference was that she stopped spending her energy on names that could never say yes.

Her manager put it in one line during the pipeline review: qualifying is not admin work you do before selling. It is the selling.

questions.q: Why did the first week produce poor results?
options: She called at the wrong times

questions.q: How many prospects were genuinely worth calling?
options: Fourteen, and nine with a known decision maker

questions.q: What did she do differently in the second week?
options: Called the qualified nine twice each at different times

questions.q: What is the manager's main point?
options: Qualifying is part of selling, not preparation for it
